claims.text: Maintaining the substrate at 200–300 °C during deposition will produce a thicker FeCoNiCrAl bond coat than deposition on a room-temperature substrate.
Substrate preheating to 200–300 °C will enhance splat spreading.
Substrate preheating to 200–300 °C will enhance inter-splat bonding.
The preheated deposition process will preserve coating integrity.
The preheated deposition process will maintain minimal coating oxidation.
Reduced thermal gradients between molten droplets and the preheated substrate cause improved splat spreading and inter-splat fusion.
Reducing the temperature differential at droplet impact promotes more effective splat flattening.
Reducing the temperature differential at droplet impact promotes splat fusion.
Enhanced inter-layer bonding increases deposit build-up and coating thickness.
An inert argon environment maintains low oxidation during preheated deposition.
Preheating will produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness relative to the room-temperature baseline.
The preheated deposit will exhibit excellent integrity.
The preheated deposit will exhibit uniformly minimal oxidation.
Room-temperature deposition using standard spray conditions yields a coating thickness of 15–45 μm.
Room-temperature baseline coatings have acceptable oxidation levels.
The benefits of substrate preheating should remain effective under standard inert-atmosphere thermal-spray conditions.
Temperatures outside 200–300 °C or substantial changes to other spray parameters may diminish the benefits or introduce defects.
Prior literature supports improved bonding and deposition efficiency from substrate preheating.

contradictions.description: The material-initial-state field identifies 15–45 μm as the feedstock particle-size distribution, whereas the baseline field reuses 15–45 μm as the deposited coating-thickness range. These are different quantities, and no coating-thickness baseline is otherwise established.
